raw_text:
Transcaval access is a percutaneous, transfemoral venous strategy for delivering large-bore devices into the abdominal aorta when conventional iliofemoral arterial access is unsafe or impossible. Its relevance has grown with the expansion of transcatheter structural heart therapy from inoperable and high-risk aortic stenosis to intermediate- and low-risk populations, because contemporary programs must still manage patients with prohibitive peripheral arterial disease, small-caliber vessels, circumferential calcification, prior vascular surgery, or hostile thoracic access anatomy [1-8].

The technique was developed primarily for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Pre-procedural computed tomography identifies a calcium-free right aortic wall target adjacent to the inferior vena cava (IVC), avoiding interposed bowel, renal vessels, pedunculated atheroma, dissection, and sites that would preclude covered-stent bailout [9,10,14]. Under fluoroscopy, a caval guiding catheter is aligned with an aortic snare. An electrified 0.014-inch guidewire traverses from the IVC, across the retroperitoneum, into the aorta and is snared; the tract is then exchanged to a stiff rail, permitting advancement of a standard large-bore introducer sheath from the femoral vein into the aorta [12,26]. After the structural intervention, the aorto-caval tract is closed, historically with off-label nitinol occluders such as Amplatzer duct or muscular ventricular septal defect occluders, with adjunctive balloon tamponade or covered stenting reserved for extravasation or intolerable shunt [12,13,18,30].

The physiologic premise is counterintuitive but clinically important: after a matched aortic and caval fenestration, arterial bleeding preferentially decompresses into the low-pressure venous system rather than accumulating freely in the retroperitoneum. This explains why a residual aorto-caval fistula can often be tolerated and later thrombose [9,13,18]. Initial human experience in 19 otherwise ineligible patients demonstrated technical feasibility, while subsequent reports extended the concept to special situations including aortic insufficiency, polyester aortic graft traversal, duplicated IVC, and left-sided venous access [9,11,15,16,28].

The pivotal prospective multicenter NHLBI study of 100 patients established the modern safety signal. Transcaval access was successful in nearly all cases, with high TAVR success and no deaths directly attributed to access, although bleeding, transfusion, and vascular complications remained common in this early experience using nondedicated closure devices [13]. One-year follow-up was reassuring: most fistulas were occluded on computed tomography, persistent patency was rare, and there were no late major transcaval vascular complications, device fractures, or migrations [18]. These data shifted the discussion from feasibility to optimization: improved patient selection, standardized CT planning, meticulous closure technique, and dedicated closure technology [14,19,26].

Comparative evidence remains observational. Single-center and multicenter studies suggest that transcaval TAVR provides outcomes at least comparable with other nonfemoral strategies, while preserving transfemoral-like operator ergonomics and avoiding thoracotomy, carotid manipulation, and brachial plexus risk [20-23]. In an 8-center propensity-weighted analysis, transcaval access had lower stroke or transient ischemic attack than transaxillary access, with similar bleeding, vascular complications, length of stay, and survival [20]. Meta-analyses report high procedural success and acceptable 30-day outcomes, but confidence intervals remain wide because published cohorts are small, selected, and center-experience dependent [17,24,25].

Patient selection is central. Favorable anatomy includes an aorta-IVC apposition zone with an adequate calcium-free window, no critical interposed structures, adequate sheath working length from femoral vein to target, and a feasible endovascular bailout plan [10,14,26]. Relative hazards include porcelain abdominal aorta, target proximity to renal arteries or the aortoiliac bifurcation, interposed bowel, mobile atheroma, chronic dissection, severe coagulopathy, and severe right-sided heart failure or pulmonary hypertension that may not tolerate acute left-to-right shunting [26]. Importantly, transcaval access should be regarded as a planned heart-team procedure rather than a desperate bailout, except in selected emergent mechanical circulatory support scenarios [26,27].

Beyond TAVR, transcaval access is conceptually attractive for other structural and large-bore cardiovascular interventions. It has been used for thoracic endovascular aortic repair and for Impella microaxial pump delivery when peripheral arterial access would risk limb ischemia or is anatomically impossible [17,26,27]. These applications emphasize a broader principle: transcaval access is not merely an alternative TAVR route, but a platform for percutaneous large-bore aortic access in patients with prohibitive arterial anatomy.

Current limitations include the need for operator training, careful CT reconstruction, familiarity with transcatheter electrosurgery, and immediate availability of covered stents and large-balloon tamponade. The absence of widely available purpose-built crossing and closure devices has slowed dissemination; early dedicated closure-device testing showed more immediate hemostasis and less access-related bleeding, but broader validation and commercialization remain important [19,26]. Contemporary consensus statements therefore recommend individualized, CT-driven selection of alternative access, favoring extrathoracic approaches and institutional expertise, with transcaval considered a core option at experienced centers [29].

In summary, transcaval access has evolved from an ingenious solution for “no-access” TAVR into a reproducible, CT-planned, fully percutaneous large-bore access strategy. Its best-supported indication remains TAVR in patients unsuitable for transfemoral arterial access and poor candidates for intrathoracic approaches. With standardized technique, careful selection, and improved closure tools, transcaval access may occupy an increasingly important role across structural heart and advanced percutaneous circulatory-support interventions.
